Texture without a mean: a diffusion model for turbulent channel-flow fields, and how to measure one

A denoising diffusion model with half a million weights, trained for 22 minutes on 5,200 planes of a turbulent channel, generates fields with streaks and wall layers of the right size and a mean velocity that is flat where the real flow rises from the walls to a core. Against an independent-pixel baseline it wins on every spatial statistic; against the training ensemble it loses on all of them. No sample is a copy of a training field, and with the distance calibrated on new real fields the samples are still farther from the training set than a new field would be. A cosine noise schedule trained in full gives the mean profile its shape and cuts its error by two thirds, at the price of a fluctuation profile that is now too high, and ten deterministic sampling steps cost a fiftieth of a second per field for the linear model with no loss, and for the cosine model with all of its gain.

Objective

Every other project in this portfolio asks a network for one answer: a field, a coefficient, a forecast. A generative model is asked for something else, a distribution: new turbulent fields that are statistically like the real ones without being any of them. Such fields would serve as inflow planes, as training data, or as an ensemble for uncertainty. The question here is whether a small denoising diffusion model trained on channel-flow planes produces fields worth that use, and how that is measured. The work is three stages, each a notebook:

  1. Stage 1 — A diffusion model for channel-flow fields: training, sampling, schedules and conditioning. A time-conditioned U-Net learns to predict the noise added to 5,200 planes of u at 200 noise levels; sampling runs the process backwards from pure noise. Then: an independent-pixel Gaussian baseline, a model conditioned on the wall shear stress, DDIM sampling with 10 to 50 steps, two noise schedules, and spectra.
  2. Stage 2 — Field statistics against held-out fields, a copying test and the cost of sampling. Every statistic scored against the 577 held-out fields with the training fields as the real-to-real reference: profiles, the velocity distribution, spectra, two-point correlations; the distance from each sample to its nearest training field; and the cost of each sampler against its quality.
  3. Stage 3 — The cosine schedule at full training, three seeds, and a calibrated copying test. The two questions Stage 2 left open: the cosine schedule trained for the full 40 epochs with three seeds and scored on the same held-out fields, and the copying test with a distance that means something, how far a new real field of this flow lies from the training set when its own snapshot is excluded.

The base training, 22 minutes on the Apple GPU, runs once; the four shorter trainings of the extensions, the three cosine trainings of Stage 3 and every sampler are repeated with seeds 0, 1 and 2. The data are the same channel-flow planes as my U-Net project, so this repository points at that release.

Problem statement

Learn the distribution of u(y, x) planes from a turbulent channel at Re_τ ≈ 125 well enough to draw new ones. Then answer three things a user of such fields would ask: are the generated fields statistically right, in their mean and fluctuation profiles, their spectrum and their spatial correlation; are they new, or copies of training fields; and what does a sample cost.

Method

Forward process, noise schedule, denoiser

The forward process adds Gaussian noise to a field in T = 200 steps with a linear variance schedule β_t from 1e-4 to 0.02; after t steps a field keeps a share ᾱ_t of its signal variance. The network is trained to predict the noise that was added, at a random step per sample, with a mean squared error; sampling starts from pure noise and removes the predicted noise step by step, adding a little fresh noise at each step (DDPM), or takes fewer, larger deterministic steps (DDIM).

References and measures

The Gaussian baseline draws every pixel independently from a normal distribution with the mean and standard deviation of the training fields at that height. It has the right profiles by construction and no spatial structure at all, which makes it the reference that separates the two kinds of error. Stage 2 measures, against the 577 held-out fields: the mean and RMS profile errors, the Wasserstein distance between the distributions of u at y+ ≈ 15, the log-spectral distance over streamwise modes 1 to 64 at y+ ≈ 15, at the centre and over all rows, the small-scale energy ratio, the two-point correlation and its length, and for the copying test the RMS difference between each sample and its nearest of the 5,200 training fields. The training fields themselves, scored the same way, show how far two real ensembles sit apart.

Which device

One training step of the denoiser inside model.fit takes 589 ms on the CPU and 87 ms on the Apple GPU (batch 16, median of 30 steps after 10 warm-up steps), so the GPU trains everything here, one job at a time. Seeded GPU trainings repeated to every printed digit in the extensions; the base training did not repeat an earlier run of the same notebook, and the cause was not established.

Results 1 — What the model generates (Stage 1)

The flat mean profile is the generator's main flaw, and the schedule is the likely cause: the model never learned to denoise from pure noise, because its last training noise level still held a third of the signal. A cosine schedule, which does reach pure noise, halves the profile error in a tenth of the epochs; whether it closes the gap at 40 epochs is not tested here. Conditioning on the wall shear stress gives samples whose wall stress correlates with the condition (0.33 [0.13, 0.54] over three seeds) at a larger RMS error, and the cause of that trade was not tested either.

The two references bracket the model. Against the independent-pixel baseline, which gets the profiles right by construction, the diffusion samples win on everything spatial: a spectral distance of 0.44 against 1.33 at y+ ≈ 15, a correlation length of 0.39 against 0.07, seven times the real small-scale energy against two thousand. Against the training fields, which show what a real ensemble looks like from the held-out one, they lose everywhere: a correlation length a third of the real 1.18, a spectral distance twenty times the real-to-real 0.02, and profiles two orders of magnitude off. The model has learned the texture of turbulence and not its mean.

Copies, and the price of a sample

Mean over three sampling seeds, 256 samples each; the three DDIM step counts are within 0.001 of each other on the profiles.
SamplerNetwork callsSeconds per sampleMean-profile errorRMS-profile errorSpectral distance at y+ ≈ 15
DDPM 2002000.2550.1930.0300.44
DDIM 50500.0730.2160.0310.48
DDIM 20200.0280.2150.0310.45
DDIM 10100.0140.2150.0320.42

No sample is a copy: the closest any of the 768 comes to a training field is 0.217, eight times the median distance of a real held-out field. But that comparison needs its caveat. The held-out fields sit so close to training fields because the random split put neighbouring planes of the same snapshots into training, so 0.026 is what a near-duplicate looks like, not what a new field looks like. The test shows the samples are not copies; it does not show they are realistic new fields. The 768 samples also have only 13 distinct nearest training fields, 455 of them the same one, which says the samples cluster where the training set is dense.

On cost, the stochastic 200-step sampler is the only one that lowers the profile error, by 0.02, at 18 times the price of DDIM 10. Ten deterministic steps give the same profile as 50, and their spectral distance is not worse. For fields this far from the real profile, the sampler is not where the quality is decided.

Results 3 — The cosine schedule at full training, and what a new field looks like (Stage 3)

Three cosine models against the base model

Stage 1's schedule comparison was ten epochs and 64 samples scored against all fields. Stage 3 trains the denoiser with the cosine schedule for the full 40 epochs, three times, and scores 256 DDPM samples per model against the 577 held-out fields with Stage 2's statistics. Because the cosine schedule ends at ᾱ ≈ 0, the sampler's clean-field estimate is clipped to the training range at each step; applied to the base model the clipping changes nothing (0.1925 either way), so the comparison is of schedules.

Cosine models: median over three training seeds, DDPM 200; base model: one training, 256 samples of this run, which reproduce Stage 2 to three decimals.

The schedule was the cause of the flat profile, and fixing it is not the whole answer. With a schedule that reaches pure noise the mean profile takes the right shape, the velocity distribution at y+ ≈ 15 moves to within 0.065 of the real one, and the two-point correlation improves at both heights. But the fluctuation profile, which the base model had nearly right, is now too high everywhere; the small-scale energy doubles its excess; the spectra do not move; and a mean-profile error of 0.068 is still a hundred times the real-to-real 0.0007. The three cosine models also disagree with each other far more than the base model's sampling seeds did (0.043 to 0.084 on the mean profile, 0.44 to 0.72 on the spectrum), which says the base model's single training is a less certain number than its sampling range suggested. And the ten-step DDIM sampler, which cost the linear model only 0.02, costs the cosine model its whole gain: 0.230 against 0.068.

What a new field looks like

Stage 2's copying test compared the samples with held-out real fields that, because of the random split, each had a neighbouring plane of the same snapshot in training. Stage 3 asks the better question: how far is a held-out field from the training fields of other snapshots?

RMS difference of u over the 201 × 384 grid to the nearest of the 5,200 training fields.
EnsembleFieldsNearest-training distance, median (range)Distinct nearest fields
Held-out real, any training field5770.026 (0.018 – 0.052)—
Held-out real, other snapshots only5770.109 (0.090 – 0.124)—
Cosine model samples, DDPM 2007680.169 (0.122 – 0.224)450
Base model samples, DDPM 2002560.229 (0.218 – 0.239)13 of 768 in Stage 2

A new real field of this flow lies about 0.11 from the training set. No sample comes closer than the closest new field (0.090), one of the 768 cosine samples falls inside the new-field range, and the rest sit farther away: the samples are not copies, and they are still less like the training set than a new real field would be, which is the other way of saying they are not yet realistic. The cosine models' samples are closer to that band than the base model's and far more diverse: their nearest training fields are 450 distinct planes, where the base model's 768 samples had 13.

Key observations

  1. A generative model needs two references, not one. An independent-pixel Gaussian baseline has the right profiles and no structure; the training fields show what a real ensemble looks like. The diffusion samples beat the first on structure and lose to the second on everything, and only the pair of comparisons says so.
  2. Texture is easier than the mean. The samples have streaks and wall layers of the right size (spectral distance 0.44 against the baseline's 1.33) and a mean profile that is flat where the real one rises from 0 to 1.06.
  3. The schedule sets the mean, and fixing it is not the whole answer. The linear schedule never reaches pure noise (ᾱ_T = 0.132) while sampling starts there; a cosine schedule trained for the full 40 epochs cuts the mean-profile error from 0.193 to 0.068 and gives the profile its shape, but raises the fluctuation profile above the real one everywhere, leaves the spectra unchanged, and loses its gain under ten-step DDIM sampling.
  4. A copying test needs a calibrated distance. Held-out real fields sit 0.026 from the training set because the split put their neighbouring planes in training; with their own snapshots excluded they sit 0.109, and that is what a new field looks like. No sample is closer than the closest new field, and most are farther: not copies, and not yet realistic.
  5. One training is one draw. The base model's seed spread is unknown, and the same notebook gave a different training loss curve in an earlier run despite its seed. The three cosine trainings of Stage 3 show how wide a training spread can be, 0.043 to 0.084 on the mean profile, so every claim that rests on the base model's single training carries an unmeasured uncertainty of about that size.
  6. Ten DDIM steps are enough for the linear model and not for the cosine one. 0.014 seconds per sample against 0.255, with the same profile error as 50 steps for the base model; with the cosine schedule the same ten steps give 0.230 against 0.068, so the step count a model can afford depends on its schedule.

Conclusion

A small diffusion model trained for 22 minutes on 5,200 channel-flow planes learns the spatial texture of near-wall turbulence, with streaks and wall layers of the right size, and not its mean: its fields are uniform across the channel where the real flow has a high-speed core. Measured properly, against held-out fields with an independent-pixel baseline on one side and the training ensemble on the other, the samples are better than noise with the right profiles and far from real. They are not copies, and ten deterministic sampling steps produce them at a fiftieth of a second each.

Stage 3 settles the two points Stage 2 left open and opens one. The cosine schedule, trained for the full 40 epochs with three seeds, gives the mean profile its shape and cuts its error by two thirds, improves the velocity distribution and the two-point correlation beyond the seed range, and does nothing for the spectra while pushing the fluctuation profile too high; it needs the full 200-step sampler to keep any of that. With the copying distance calibrated on held-out fields from other snapshots, the samples are confirmed not to be copies and shown to be farther from the training set than a new real field, the cosine model's closer and far more diverse than the base model's.

What the stages do not establish: the base model's training-seed spread, which the cosine models suggest is not small; why the cosine models over-fluctuate, and whether a longer training or a different T corrects it; why the conditional model trades a larger error for its correlation with the wall stress; and whether a sampler between 10 and 200 steps keeps the cosine model's gain. The next steps are the base model retrained with three seeds, a DDIM step sweep for the cosine model, and a held-out spectrum and correlation at every height rather than two.
